problem.title: A durable key-value store for a small cluster
problem.context: Three nodes in one region keep configuration data that every service reads at start-up.

requirements.text: Every committed write is visible on all nodes.
No committed write is lost when one node fails.
The team already runs everything on S3.

approaches.idea: What if each node kept the truth on its own disk?
What if the truth lived in S3, where the team already is?

points.description: Local disks with a quorum and an explicit commit protocol.
A shared log in S3 as the source of truth.

trajectory.hypothesis: A quorum of local disks with a commit protocol should keep every committed write when a node fails.
trajectory.observation: Durable and consistent, and a source attests the combination; it adds disks the S3 platform does not need.

tradeoffs.note: Serves requests durably, but the commit protocol adds cost.

trajectory.hypothesis: Without the commit protocol, the disk quorum alone may still be durable.
trajectory.observation: Durable, but a write is no longer visible on every node when acknowledged; nothing attests it.

tradeoffs.note: Durable on a node failure, but nothing orders concurrent writes.

trajectory.hypothesis: A log in S3 should be durable and fit the constraint.
trajectory.observation: Fits the platform and a source attests it; replication stays open.

tradeoffs.note: Cheap durability in S3, at the cost of request latency.

alternatives.name: Disk quorum with three-phase commit
alternatives.summary: Each node keeps the data on its own disk; writes commit on a quorum.

choices.reason: A quorum of disks survives one node failure.
Three-phase commit makes a write visible on every node before it is acknowledged.

considered.reason: A WAL in S3 fits the platform, but adds a dependency on S3 for every write.

relations.note: Keeping the truth on local disks is what makes a commit protocol between nodes necessary.

alternatives.name: WAL in S3
alternatives.summary: The nodes write a log to S3 and rebuild their state from it.

choices.reason: S3 is already the team's durable store.

open.reason: With the log in S3, no requirement decides how the nodes replicate.

adrs.title: Where the source of truth lives
adrs.context: No committed write may be lost when a node fails, and the team already runs everything on S3.

options.name: A quorum of local disks
pros: Survives one node failure without any external service.
cons: Adds disks to run next to S3.
options.reason: Durability without depending on S3 for every write.

options.name: A write-ahead log in S3
pros: Uses the platform the team already runs.

adrs.title: How replicas agree on a write
adrs.context: With the truth on local disks, a write must be visible on every node before it is acknowledged.

options.name: Three-phase commit
pros: A write is visible on every node when acknowledged.
options.reason: R1 asks for every committed write on all nodes.

options.name: Another replication scheme
cons: Does not make writes visible everywhere at once.

comparison.note: A1 keeps the truth on the nodes' disks; A2 keeps it in S3.
A1 needs three-phase commit; A2 leaves replication open.
